description: CSLabs is a technology-driven team passionate about AI, robotics, and software engineering. For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to develop an intelligent health monitoring solution for astronauts, using AI and data analysis to track health indicators, identify potential risks, and support decision-making during space missions.
summary:
Astronauts going to Mars will be far from any doctor: a call for help takes up to 22 minutes to reach Earth, and as long to come back. SONQO is health monitoring software that watches each astronaut without contact (camera, radar, thermal and depth sensors, plus a simple wristband), learns their personal normal with a digital twin, and alarms only when two sensors agree. Its "My status" screen explains what is happening and what to do; the astronaut always decides. Only the unexpected travels to Earth, in a 30-byte card, and every decision goes into a black box Earth can verify. We built a working prototype for a crew of four, with a talking assistant and live wristbands. We also introduce ARCA, our next step: an on-board medical capsule where SONQO moves from warning to acting, only after the astronaut's "yes".

How NASA data helped us: NASA-STD-3001 puts Mars missions at Level V, its most autonomous medical care, so SONQO decides on board. NASA's Mars delay studies (3 to 22 minutes one way, two-week blackouts at solar conjunction) sized the 30-byte card and the delayed link. The Integrated Medical Model's ~100 conditions support our N0–N4 autonomy levels, and Curiosity's RAD dose fills the card's radiation field. Signals are still simulated; the app's "NASA data" section shows each source.
details:
What it does. SONQO measures pulse, breathing and skin temperature without anything touching the astronaut. It compares each value with that astronaut's own normal, not with a population average. When two different sensors agree that a value has left the normal range, SONQO tells the astronaut what is happening and recommends what to do. Anything at autonomy level N2 or above needs the astronaut's "yes". With that "yes", a 30-byte alert card is sent to Earth.

How it works.

  1. Energy cascade E0–E3: at rest only the radar watches (about 2 W). If it sees a change, the thermal camera wakes up, and to confirm, the color camera and the depth camera turn on for a few seconds. The camera is truly released when it is not needed.
  2. Contactless pulse from the color camera, with the classic POS algorithm (Wang et al., 2017): skin regions of the forehead and cheeks, band-pass filter, spectrum peak and a quality score. No heavy neural networks.
  3. Two sources must agree (within 5 bpm) before any alarm. If they disagree, SONQO verifies first and does not alarm the astronaut.
  4. Personal digital twin: it learns each crew member's normal band, predicts the next 60 s (Kalman filter) and gives a calibrated interval (conformal prediction). It does not learn from deviations, so a long episode never becomes "normal".
  5. Rules engine with autonomy levels N0–N4, set before the mission by flight surgeons. Nothing at N2 runs without the astronaut's "yes" on the "My status" screen.
  6. T-30 card: a whole emergency in 30 bytes with a CRC, sent in 4 copies over a delayed link. On Earth it is decoded field by field and arrives byte-identical.
  7. Black box: every reading and decision goes into a SHA-256 hash chain. Anyone can check that nothing was edited and replay the log to get the same decision.

The system. The software monitors the whole crew of four (MS-1 to MS-4). Each crew member has a live view with their values against their own normal, their last minutes, their routine measurements and their own black box. Each also has their own "My status" screen, where only they can say "yes". The SONQO assistant is a sphere you can talk or type to, with the four crew wristbands orbiting it live. It answers from the system's live data ("How is MS-3?", "Did the alert reach Earth?", "Verify MS-1's black box"). It warns by itself when someone leaves their normal, and it refuses to authorize anything on the astronaut's behalf. It is rule-based, not a language model: it does not make things up and it works offline. It speaks with a local neural voice. The ARCA view shows who authorized it and its usage history, read from the black boxes.

Wristband add-on. The module sensors only see the astronaut when they are in front of them. A simple wristband (wrist PPG pulse and vibration, no screen, own battery) follows them while they sleep, exercise or move between modules. It is one more source in the two-sensor rule, so it can confirm or contradict the radar. It also vibrates to tell the astronaut to check "My status" when SONQO recommends something. In the sandbox it is simulated, like the other sensors.

ARCA, the next step. We also designed ARCA, an on-board medical capsule that takes SONQO from warning to acting. It is a design concept with technical documentation (version 3.2): a 377 kg capsule with two anchored robotic arms that swap eight tools on their own (venipuncture, ultrasound, compression, irrigation, dressing, skin closure, cutting and forceps), X-ray and head MRI, and walls that reuse the mission's water as shielding against solar storms. It acts alone only inside short, pre-approved protocols; everything else needs the astronaut's "yes". In the documentation's simulation, autonomous treatment starts at minute 2.5, versus minute 50.4 when waiting for Earth with Mars at its farthest. ARCA is not part of the software prototype; it is shown as an AI-generated video with a watermark.

Benefits. The astronaut understands their state and acts in minutes instead of waiting for Earth. The link carries only a few bytes. Every automatic decision can be audited. The same logic (measure, explain, recommend, notify) can serve rural health posts in the Andes and the Amazon, with few doctors and intermittent connectivity.

What we hope to achieve. By May 14, 2027, validate that SONQO measures contactless pulse with a mean error of 5 bpm or less against a pulse oximeter in 10 volunteers with different skin tones. It should also detect a deviation confirmed by two sensors within 20 s, send the alert in 30 bytes and average 4 W or less per module.

What is real and what is simulated. The software, algorithms, twin, energy cascade, T-30 encoder, delayed channel and black box are real code with 55 automated tests. In the sandbox, the radar, thermal and depth sensors and the wristband are simulated, and the camera input is a public face video. Only MS-2 has a camera; MS-1, MS-3 and MS-4 run the same logic on simulated sensors. Every simulated source is labeled "simulated" on screen. Clinical rules are illustrative: this is not a medical device. ARCA, an on-board medical capsule, is a team concept with technical documentation; in the prototype it appears only as a video.

Tools. Python 3.11, FastAPI, Uvicorn and WebSocket, NumPy, SciPy, OpenCV and MediaPipe Face Mesh. The interface is plain JavaScript, canvas and WebGL with no CDNs, and it works offline. The assistant's optional voice is IndexTTS-2.5, a neural text-to-speech model running locally. Interface in English and Spanish.
